But this is a low-ceiling advice. It gets students out of the habit of summarizing, but it does not teach them how to write well. It does not teach them how to use telling effectively. It does not teach them that telling can be powerful, precise, and essential. It creates a generation of writers who are terrified of their own voices. They hide behind descriptions. They avoid making direct statements. They avoid arguing. They avoid reflecting. They produce prose that is visually dense but intellectually shallow.

The best writers know when to show and when to tell. They know that showing is for the moment, for the immediate, for the physical. They know that telling is for the context, for the reflection, for the idea. They know that a novel is not just a series of scenes. It is an argument. It is a meditation. It is a conversation between the author and the reader. And conversations require statements. They require summaries. They require judgments.

If you want to write well, stop treating “telling” as a sin. Learn to tell clearly. Learn to tell with precision. Learn to tell with style. Because if you can’t tell, you can’t show either. You can only describe. And description, without the anchor of the narrator’s voice, is just a list of objects.

prompt: for my newsletter (mostly librarians and teachers, ~3k subscribers): an essay on rereading. why the second time through a book is often the first time you actually read it. warm but not twee, 800ish words
chosen:
**The Second Time Is the First Time**

There is a specific, quiet thrill that comes not from the first page of a new book, but from the first page of an old one.

For librarians and teachers, we are often the curators of the "new." We stand at the front tables with the latest releases, we chase the syllabus deadlines, and we guide students toward their next great discovery. We are in the business of novelty. But if you are like me, the most profound reading experiences of your life likely happened in the margins of a book you had already read.

We tend to think of rereading as a repetition, a lazy echo of a past pleasure. But I would argue that the second time through is often the first time you actually read.

When we encounter a book for the first time, we are in survival mode. We are scanning for plot points, decoding vocabulary, tracking character motivations, and trying to figure out where the story is going. We are tourists in a foreign city, looking up at the architecture, checking the map, wondering what’s around the corner. We are busy processing the *what* and the *how*.

But when you return to a book, the map is already in your pocket. You know how it ends. You know who survives and who doesn’t. You know the twist coming three chapters from now. And because you don’t have to worry about the destination, you are finally free to look at the scenery.

This shift in cognitive load changes everything.

I remember rereading *The Great Gatsby* in my late twenties. The first time, in high school, I was stressed about the test. I was worried about Nick Carraway’s voice and the symbolism of the green light. The second time, I wasn’t thinking about symbols. I was thinking about the feeling of being young and believing that money could buy back time. I noticed details I had completely missed before: the specific shade of blue in the eyes, the way the party guests looked at Gatsby with a mixture of awe and revulsion. I wasn’t analyzing the text; I was inhabiting it.

For educators, this is a crucial lesson to pass on. We often tell students that rereading is just "doing it again." We frame it as a requirement for comprehension checks or essay preparation. But if we could reframe rereading as an act of deepening, rather than repetition, we might change how our students relate to literature.

Rereading is where the dialogue with the author truly begins. The first read is the author speaking to you. The second read is you speaking back. You notice the author’s silences. You wonder why a character said that thing in that specific way. You catch the irony you missed because you were too busy following the plot. You see the structure, the rhythm, the architecture of the sentences.

And then there is the element of time.

This is the part that often goes unspoken in our profession, but it is the heart of the matter. When you reread a book, you are not just the same person who read it the first time. You have lived. You have aged. You have suffered, succeeded, loved, and lost.

The book hasn’t changed, but you have. And so, the meaning of the book changes.

I reread *To Kill a Mockingbird* after becoming a father. The first time, I saw Atticus Finch as a paragon of moral courage. The second time, I saw him as a man trapped in a community that demanded he be a symbol rather than a person. I saw the weight of his silence. I saw the cost of standing up for what is right when everyone around you is telling you it’s wrong. The text was identical, but the subtext had shifted because my life had shifted.

This is why I encourage my students to keep their books. I tell them: "You are not done with this book until you are done with the chapter of your life that this book was speaking to."

In a world of infinite content, of endless new releases and algorithmic recommendations, rereading is a radical act of depth. It is a rejection of the idea that we must always be consuming something new to be growing. Sometimes, growth looks like turning back. Sometimes, understanding looks like sitting with what you already know until it reveals something new.

So, the next time you find yourself reaching for the "New Releases" shelf, pause. Look at the book on your nightstand that you read five years ago. The one that has the cracked spine and the faded cover.

Pick it up. Open it to a random page.

You won’t be reading it the same way twice. And that is exactly the point.
rejected:
**The First Time Is Just the Entry Ticket**

There is a specific, quiet kind of anxiety that comes with opening a book for the second time. It’s not the fear of not remembering the plot, though that can happen. It’s the fear that the magic is gone. You’ve seen the ending. You know who dies, who gets away with it, and which subplots are red herrings and which are the main course. The mystery is solved. The surprise is dead.

So why do we do it? Why do we go back to *The Great Gatsby* or *Beloved* or *Pride and Prejudice*?

We go back because the first time we read a book, we were usually too busy to actually read it.

Think about your first pass through a significant novel. You were likely young, or at least younger than you are now. Your brain was running at a frantic pace, processing the plot like a video game: *What happens next? Who is the villain? Does the hero survive the cliffhanger?* We are wired for narrative propulsion. We are tourists in a foreign country, snapping photos of the landmarks, checking the boxes, worrying about catching the train to the next city. We are skimming for the story.

But rereading is different. Rereading is when you stop being a tourist and start being a resident.

When you open a book for the second time, the narrative engine is no longer the primary driver. You aren’t holding your breath to see if the character makes it off the ledge; you already know they do. This liberation allows you to finally look at the room around the ledge. You start to notice the author’s syntax. You catch the subtle shifts in tone that you missed when you were sprinting toward the climax. You begin to hear the music of the language rather than just the lyrics of the plot.

There is a reason librarians and teachers are the first to champion the value of the second read. In the classroom, we often treat books as vehicles for information transfer or moral lessons. We ask, "What is the theme?" and "What is the message?" But a reread reveals the texture of the human experience. It shows us that a character’s decision wasn’t just a plot point, but a complex, messy, contradictory act of being human.

Consider *The Catcher in the Rye*. The first time you read it, you’re likely angry at Holden Caulfield. You think he’s a whiny, arrogant teenager who needs to grow up. You’re focused on his behavior. The second time, often after you’ve lived a few years of adulthood yourself, you stop looking at his behavior and start looking at his pain. You realize he isn’t performing for an audience; he’s trying to survive. The anger softens into empathy. The book doesn’t change, but you have.

This is the secret of rereading: the book is a mirror, not a window. The first time, you look out the window at the scenery. The second time, you see your own reflection in the glass.

For those of us who work with books, this distinction is crucial. We spend a lot of time recommending books based on what they *do* to the reader. We talk about plot twists, character arcs, and historical context. But we rarely talk about the slow, sedimentary way a book settles into your bones over time. A book you read at sixteen is a different object than the one you reread at thirty-six. The words are identical, but the meaning is entirely different because the decoder has changed.

This is why we should normalize rereading. It’s not a lack of discipline. It’s not that you didn’t read the book properly the first time. It’s that the first time was just the entry ticket. The second time is when you actually get to sit down and have a conversation with the author.

There is also a comfort in the familiarity of a reread. In a world that is often loud, fast, and unpredictable, returning to a known text is an act of grounding. You know the layout. You know where the quiet moments are. You can pause on a specific page and let it breathe, without the pressure of needing to find out what happens next. It is a low-stakes, high-reward experience. It is the literary equivalent of putting on a favorite sweater. It doesn’t impress you; it holds you.

So, if you are holding a book on your nightstand that you finished six months ago, and you think you’ve "done" it, I have a gentle challenge for you. Put it down. Wait a month. Let your life change a little. Let a new grief or a new joy or a new perspective settle in. Then, open it again.

Don’t rush to the end. Don’t worry about the plot. Just read a page. Let the words wash over you. You might be surprised to find that the first time you actually read it, was this time.

The first time is for the story. The second time is for the soul.

prompt: Is Moby-Dick boring on purpose? Essay.
chosen:
It is a common complaint that *Moby-Dick* is tedious. Readers who find the cetology chapters, the whaling diagrams, or the digressions on the harpoon head dull are not wrong to feel that way. But the idea that Melville wrote the book to be boring—that he was deliberately stalling for time or mocking the reader’s patience—misses the point entirely. The boredom is not the goal; it is the cost of entry.

Melville was not writing a thriller. He was writing a philosophical epic about a man who is trying to impose meaning on a universe that offers none. The novel is structured as a series of attempts to understand the whale. Ishmael and Ahab try to understand it through science, through religion, through history, and through psychology. Each of these approaches fails. The whale remains an enigma.

The "boring" parts are where those approaches are laid out in detail. When Melville spends forty pages on the anatomy of the whale, he is not just showing off his research. He is demonstrating the limits of human categorization. You can dissect the animal, measure its bones, and name its organs, but you cannot capture its essence. The tedium is the feeling of hitting that wall. It is the experience of looking at something vast and indifferent and finding no purchase for your mind.

Ahab’s obsession is not just with killing the whale; it is with making the whale say something. He wants the white whale to be a symbol, a sign, a message. But the whale refuses to be a symbol. It is just a whale. The long, dense passages of the book mirror this refusal. They are dense because the whale is dense. They are opaque because the truth is opaque.

If Melville had written a tight, fast-paced story about a ship chasing a shark, it would have been a different book. It might have been exciting. But it would not have been *Moby-Dick*. The boredom is the texture of the real. It is the weight of the ocean. It is the time it takes to grind the whale oil. It is the slow, grinding realization that the world is much larger and much stranger than our stories can hold.

So, is it boring on purpose? No. It is boring because it is true. The universe does not move at the speed of a plot twist. It moves at the speed of tides, of rot, of slow geological change. Melville forced the reader to sit with that slowness. If you push through the tedium, you find that the boredom was the point. It was the only way to make you feel the size of the thing Ahab was chasing.
rejected:
No. *Moby-Dick* is not boring on purpose. It is boring because it is a massive, encyclopedic, and often digressive work that prioritizes intellectual and aesthetic ambition over narrative momentum. To call it "boring on purpose" implies a strategic deception—that Melville hid the good parts behind the bad parts to trick the reader. That is not what happens.

The book is boring in the way a cathedral is boring if you are only looking for a place to park a car. Melville constructs a labyrinth. He wants you to stand in the center of the whaling industry, the natural philosophy of the 19th century, and the metaphysics of obsession. If you only want a shark-and-hell story, you are looking for the wrong building.

### The Nature of the "Boredom"

The boredom readers feel is usually specific. It is not the boredom of poor writing. Melville’s prose is often electrifying, dense, and beautiful. The boredom is structural.

1.  **The Encyclopedia:** Chapters like "Cetology," "Anatomy," and "The Whale-Boat and Its Appurtenances" are not filler. They are the core of Melville’s artistic project. He is trying to capture the *totality* of the whale as a symbol. A whale is not just a plot device; it is a biological, economic, and mythological entity. To ignore its biology is to ignore its symbolic weight. For a reader who wants action, this is a wall. For a reader interested in how knowledge is structured, it is a marvel.
2.  **The Digression:** Ahab’s monologues are often static. He talks. Ishmael watches. Time stops. This is not a failure of pacing; it is a stylistic choice to emphasize the psychological and philosophical interiority of the character. Melville is less interested in *what happens* than in *what it means*. This creates a sense of stagnation that many readers interpret as boredom.
3.  **The Tone:** The book is relentlessly serious. It does not wink. It does not offer comic relief to break the tension of the hunt. This sustained intensity is exhausting. It demands a level of sustained attention that modern narrative fiction rarely asks for.

### Why It Feels Like a Trap

The reason the "boring on purpose" theory persists is that the book *does* start with a hook. "Call me Ishmael" is one of the most famous openings in literature. The early chapters are lively, social, and grounded in the reality of boarding a ship. Then, abruptly, the ship leaves port, and the book becomes a lecture.

This shift feels like a betrayal because the contract with the reader changes. We thought we were reading a seafaring adventure; we are now reading a philosophical treatise wrapped in an adventure. Melville knew this. He was aware that his ambitions would alienate the general public. His contemporary Herman Melville (no, wait, Melville’s contemporary Nathaniel Hawthorne) called the book "a monstrous whale," and the public initially agreed. The book was a commercial failure.

But Melville did not write it to be a commercial success. He wrote it to be a total work. He wanted to exhaust the subject. He wanted to say everything that could be said about the whale, the sea, and the human condition, all at once. The boredom is the cost of that totality.

### The Reward

If you push through the boredom, the book reveals itself as a masterpiece of structural integrity. The encyclopedic chapters are not interruptions; they are the background radiation of the narrative. They create a world so dense and real that Ahab’s madness feels inevitable. The whale is not just an animal; it is the embodiment of all the knowledge, fear, and mystery that Melville has cataloged in those "boring" chapters.

When the ship finally hits the whale, the impact is physical and philosophical because we have spent 300 pages understanding what the whale *is*. Without the "boring" parts, the climax is just a boat accident. With them, it is a collision between human reason and the indifferent universe.

### Conclusion

*Moby-Dick* is not boring on purpose. It is boring to those who want a story, because it is not primarily a story. It is an experience of saturation. It is boring in the way that reading a detailed map of a city is boring if you just want to get from A to B. But if you want to understand the city, the map is the point.

Melville’s mistake, if it is one, was assuming that readers would be willing to pay the price of entry for that understanding. Most were not. They are still not. But the boredom is not a trick. It is the texture of the book. It is the weight of the whale.

prompt: Argue that the second person ('you') is the most manipulative point of view in fiction, and that this is exactly why it works.
chosen:
The second person is not a perspective; it is an instruction.

First person is a confession. It invites empathy by sharing the burden of guilt, joy, or fear. Third person is a documentary. It invites observation by maintaining a safe distance. Both are passive modes of consumption. The reader sits in the audience or the therapist’s chair.

Second person is active. It removes the reader from the audience and places them in the body of the character. When a story says, "You walk into the room and feel the eyes on your neck," the reader’s brain cannot distinguish the narrative command from a physical sensation. This is the manipulation. It bypasses critical distance. It forces the reader to inhabit the character’s specific, often unpleasant, limitations.

This is why it is the most manipulative point of view: it claims ownership of the reader’s sensory experience. It tells you how to feel, where to look, and what to fear, and because the language is addressed directly to you, resistance feels like disloyalty. To disagree with the character’s perception is to argue with your own immediate reality.

This is also why it works so rarely and so powerfully. The technique requires a strict discipline. If the character’s actions are too heroic, the reader feels accused of cowardice. If the character is too stupid, the reader feels stupid. The author must write a character whose flaws are universal enough to be recognized but specific enough to be felt. The success of the second person relies entirely on the reader’s willingness to be uncomfortable. It trades safety for intimacy.

The manipulation is the point. Fiction usually asks, "What would you do?" The second person answers, "You are doing it. Look."
rejected:
The second-person point of view is often dismissed as a gimmick, a stylistic affectation, or a broken narrative engine. It is the "uncanny valley" of prose, creating a dissonance that can make readers feel like they are being held at gunpoint rather than invited into a story. But this discomfort is not a bug; it is the feature.

To argue that the second person is the most manipulative perspective in fiction is to argue that it is the only one that bypasses the reader’s defenses entirely. It works *because* it is manipulative.

### The Illusion of Agency

In the first person ("I"), the narrator is a distinct entity. You are observing a consciousness that is separate from your own. You can empathize with "I," but you are not "I." You can critique "I," judge "I," or detach from "I." The first person offers a safe distance.

In the third person ("He/She/They"), the distance is even greater. The character is an object of observation. You are a ghost floating above the scene. You have total freedom to look away.

In the second person ("You"), there is no distance. There is no "I" to observe and no "They" to judge. The pronoun "you" performs a sleight of hand so aggressive that most readers don’t notice the card switch until they are already holding the deck.

**"You" is not the reader. But "you" is forced to occupy the space where the reader is.**

This is the core of the manipulation: **false agency.** The text tells you, "You feel the cold rain on your face." You do not. But your brain, trained to accept linguistic input as experiential data, briefly simulates the sensation. The narrative has hijacked your sensory cortex. It has convinced you that you are the protagonist, even though you have no control over the plot, no choice in the dialogue, and no say in the outcome.

This is a power imbalance that is inherently unethical in real life, but in fiction, it is the only way to achieve total immersion. First and third person require you to *project* yourself into the story. Second person *installs* itself in you.

### The Complicity of the Reader

The second person does not just manipulate perception; it manipulates moral responsibility.

When a first-person narrator commits an act of violence or betrayal, the reader can distance themselves: "That’s what *he* did." The reader remains a witness.

When a second-person character does the same thing, the reader becomes a participant.

> *"You raise the knife. You look at her. You hesitate. Then you cut."*

By the time the blade falls, the reader has been complicit. The use of "you" creates a sense of shared guilt or shared shame that is almost impossible to replicate in any other mode. The reader cannot look away because the narrative has pinned them to the page with the pronoun. It is an act of narrative coercion.

This is why second-person fiction is so rare and so polarizing. It demands that the reader surrender their autonomy. It says: *You will feel this. You will think this. You will be ashamed of this. You cannot opt out.*

### Why This Is Why It Works

If the second person were merely a descriptive tool, it would be inefficient. Why say "You see the tree" when "The tree stood tall" is more elegant?

The second person works precisely because it is a **trap of intimacy.**

1.  **It eliminates the "observer effect."** In first and third person, the reader is always aware they are reading a story. In second person, that awareness is suppressed by the direct address. The narrative speaks to you as if you are in the room. This breaks the fourth wall not by acknowledging the fiction, but by pretending the fiction is reality.
2.  **It creates immediate empathy through identification.** You cannot empathize with a stranger as quickly as you can with yourself. By making the reader the protagonist, the second person short-circuits the empathetic process. You don’t have to *try* to understand the character; you *are* the character. The emotional response is instantaneous and visceral.
3.  **It forces engagement.** The second person is confrontational. It does not ask for your attention; it seizes it. This is why it is so effective in horror, thriller, and confessional fiction. The tension is not just in the plot; it is in the psychological pressure of being told what you are feeling.

### The Ethical Ambiguity

This is why the second person is the most dangerous point of view. It is a form of narrative violence. It violates the reader’s sovereignty.

Consider *The House in the Cerulean Sea* or *A Monster Calls*. In *A Monster Calls*, the second person is used to place the reader in the position of a dying boy. The manipulation is not malicious; it is empathetic. But it is still a force. The reader is made to feel the weight of mortality not as an observer, but as a participant.

Or consider the second-person short story *The Head* by Robert McCammon, where the reader is forced to confront their own complicity in a crime. The discomfort is the point. The manipulation is the message.

### Conclusion

The second person is not a neutral lens. It is a weapon. It is the only point of view that can claim the reader’s body, their emotions, and their moral agency without consent.

It works because it is **invasive.**

It works because it is **intimate.**

It works because it is **manipulative.**

Any other point of view asks you to imagine. The second person tells you that you are already there. And in the dark, quiet space between the words and the eye, you are.

prompt: Write a personal essay about keeping a diary for twenty years and then rereading it, and finding that the person in it is a stranger who annoys you. What is a diary for, if not for the future self?
chosen:
The tape on the spine of the 1994 notebook has cracked. It smells like mildew and something sharper, like old paper turning to dust. I bought these books because I wanted to remember what it felt like to be nineteen. I wanted to find the specific texture of my own youth.

Instead, I found a man who is insufferable.

He is not me. That is the shock. I am not the person who spent three pages analyzing why a barista gave him the wrong size coffee. I am not the person who wrote, in bold letters, *I am better than them. I am not like them.* I am not the person who fell in love with a woman named Sarah, whom I now realize was probably just a phase, but who occupied forty percent of the 1997 volume.

The stranger in the book is verbose, self-righteous, and tragically unaware of his own mediocrity. He thinks his opinions are original. He thinks his suffering is unique. He writes about his day with the gravity of a chronicler of war. I read his entries and feel a physical revulsion, the same kind I feel when I meet a colleague who talks only about his commute.

This raises a problem. A diary is traditionally defined as a record kept for the future self. It is a letter to yourself. But if the recipient of that letter is a stranger, what is the point?

If the purpose is memory, it fails. I do not remember the details of 1998. I remember the *feeling* of being in love, the *concept* of being angry. The diary gives me data, not experience. It tells me what I ate, not how the food tasted. It tells me who I argued with, not the exact cadence of my voice when I was losing. Memory is a reconstruction; the diary is a transcript. They do not match. The transcript is often worse than the memory because it captures the performance of emotion rather than the emotion itself.

If the purpose is self-improvement, it also fails. I do not want to be the person in the 1994 book. He was anxious, petty, and trying too hard. I have spent twenty years building a self that is quieter, more integrated, and less concerned with being "right." Reading his words is not a lesson; it is a confrontation with a corpse. You do not learn from a corpse. You bury it.

So what is a diary for?

Perhaps it is not for the future self at all. Perhaps it is a container for the present self. It is a place to put the thoughts that do not fit in the room. When you are in the middle of a grief, or a rage, or a joy, the feeling is too large for the body. It spills over. You need a place to put it so you can go on. The diary is a trash can for the mind. It is a drain for the pressure.

The act of writing is not communication. It is exhalation.

When I write in my current journal, I am not writing for the man who will read it in 2044. That man is already a stranger. He will have different values, different memories, different scars. He will look at my current anxieties with the same pity and confusion I look at the 1994 entries.

I write to get the thought out of my head. I write to pin it down so I can stop turning it over. I write to make it small.

The stranger in the 1994 book was doing the same thing. He was trying to make his pain small enough to hold. He was trying to make his pride safe. He was trying to survive the day.

I do not need to like him. I do not need to learn from him. I only need to acknowledge that he was there. That he was doing the work of being alive, badly, loudly, and in a language that has since changed.

I close the notebook. The smell of mildew fades. I am not him. He is not me. We are just two people who happened to occupy the same body for a stretch of time, passing a baton in the dark. He ran his leg of the race. I am running mine.

The diary is not a bridge. It is a grave marker.

The box was sitting in the attic, tucked behind a stack of out-of-season comforters and a broken toaster, as if it were trying to hide. It was a simple, hardcover thing, bound in navy blue cloth that had worn to a pale, dusty gray at the corners. I had bought it twenty years ago, in the autumn of a year that felt, at the time, like the definitive beginning of my adult life.

I had always been told that keeping a diary was an act of preservation. It was a time capsule, a letter to a future self who would need to know how it felt to be twenty-three, or thirty, or forty. The advice was consistent: *Write down your hopes, your fears, your petty grievances. Future You will thank you for the record.*

So I wrote. Every night, for twenty years, I sat at the same desk, under the same lamp, and poured myself out. I wrote about the job I hated, the partner who left, the dog who died, the promotion I didn’t get, and the slow, grinding realization that I was becoming someone I wasn’t sure I liked. I wrote with a fervor that bordered on obsession, treating the page as a confessional, a therapist, and a witness all at once.

When I finally opened the box, the smell hit me first: dust, old paper, and a faint, sweet decay. I sat on the attic floor, my knees pulled up to my chest, and opened the first volume.

The handwriting was the first shock. It was slanted, hurried, and illegible in places, a scrawl that looked less like writing and more like the frantic scratching of a bird in a cage. I had forgotten how I looked. I had forgotten how I sounded.

I turned the page.

*"Dear Diary,"* it began. The salutation was a relic, a formality I had abandoned after the first few months. *"I am so angry at Mark today. He didn’t even look at me when I told him about the presentation. He just kept checking his watch. He thinks he’s so above it all. He thinks he’s the smartest person in the room, and maybe he is, but he’s a hollow, pretentious piece of work. I hate him. I want to leave. I want to burn it all down."*

I stared at the words. *Hollow, pretentious piece of work.*

The person on the page was not me. Or rather, it was me, but a version of me that I found deeply, irrationally annoying. She was loud. She was self-pitying. She was obsessed with her own suffering in a way that felt performative. She demanded attention, even from a piece of paper. She wrote in exclamation points. She used words like *absolutely* and *totally* and *insufferable* with a frequency that made my teeth ache.

I turned to a page from five years later.

*"The rain hasn’t stopped for three days. It’s pathetic. It’s just raining. I’m sitting here feeling sorry for myself because I’m alone. Why does everyone else seem to have it together? They must be lying. They’re all just pretending. I’m the only real one."*

I felt a physical flinch. This woman was a mess. She was messy in her thoughts, in her logic, in her emotional hygiene. She was dramatic to the point of fatigue. I found myself wanting to shake her, to tell her to grow up, to stop being so hard on herself and so hard on the world. I wanted to tell her that Mark wasn’t as bad as she thought, that the rain was just water, that being alone was not a moral failing.

And then I realized the most unsettling part: I didn’t miss her.

I had expected to feel a pang of nostalgia, a warm connection to the young woman who had poured her heart out. I had expected to feel a sense of continuity, a thread connecting my past self to my present one. Instead, I felt a sense of profound alienation. She was a stranger. She was a character in a book I had written but never read. I looked at her with the same detached curiosity I might look at a stranger on a train—mildly annoyed by her noise, slightly pitying of her confusion, but ultimately indifferent.

I kept reading. I skimmed through the middle years, looking for myself, looking for the person I thought I was. I found glimpses. A note about a trip to Italy. A list of books I wanted to read. A brief entry about a new job. But even in these neutral moments, the voice was the same. It was a voice that was always *about* itself. *How I felt. How I reacted. How the world failed me or helped me.* There was no space for the world itself, only the world as a mirror.

I reached the final volume, the one I had kept for the last two years. I expected to find a change. I expected to find the person I was now—more grounded, more quiet, more accepting.

But it wasn’t.

*"I’m tired of trying to fix it,"* the last entry read. *"I’m tired of trying to be someone else. I’m just going to let it be."*

I closed the book. The attic was silent. The dust motes danced in the shaft of light from the small window.

I had always thought a diary was a bridge. A way to carry the past into the future, to make the past relevant, to make the future coherent. I had thought that by writing, I was building a foundation for who I would become. I had thought that Future Me would look back at Past Me and say, *Ah, I see. I understand now why I am who I am. I see the roots.*

But that wasn’t what happened.

Future Me looked at Past Me and saw a stranger. A loud, dramatic, self-absorbed stranger who didn’t know who she was yet. And the terrifying thing wasn’t that I had changed. The terrifying thing was that I hadn’t. The core of the person in the diary—the need to be heard, the need to be right, the need to be special—was still there. I just had better tools to hide it. I was quieter now. I was more polished. But the engine was the same. It was just running more smoothly.

So what is a diary for?

It is not for the future self. It is not a time capsule. It is not a letter to a friend you will one day become.

A diary is for the *now*. It is for the moment when the feeling is too big to hold, when the thought is too sharp to swallow. It is a pressure valve. It is a place to put the weight down so you can carry it for one more day. It is not meant to be read. It is meant to be *written*.

The act of writing is the point. The release of the words onto the page is the point. The diary is not a record of who you are; it is a record of what you *felt* at that specific moment in time. And feelings are ephemeral. They do not survive the passage of time. They do not translate. They are not meant to be understood by a future self who has lived through ten more winters, lost two more people, and learned two more things.

I realized that I had been keeping the diary for the wrong reason. I had been keeping it as if it were a monument to my life. But a life is not a monument. A life is a process. It is a series of moments that are only real in the instant they happen. Once they are gone, they are gone. You cannot go back to them. You can only look at the scar they left.

The person in the diary was not a stranger because she was different from me. She was a stranger because she was *finished*. She was a moment that had passed. And I was a moment that was passing. And the next moment would be a stranger to this one, too.

I closed the box. I did not put it back in the attic. I put it in the trash.

It felt wrong. It felt like a betrayal. But then I felt a lightness in my chest, a sudden, sharp clarity. I was not defined by the words I had written twenty years ago. I was not defined by the person who wrote them. I was only defined by the next word I would say, the next step I would take, the next breath I would take.

I went downstairs. I made a cup of tea. I sat at the same desk, under the same lamp, and I picked up a fresh notebook.

I didn’t write *Dear Diary*. I didn’t write about Mark, or the rain, or the hollow, pretentious piece of work. I wrote about the way the light was falling on the floor. I wrote about the sound of the traffic outside. I wrote about the taste of the tea.

I wrote for no one. I wrote for no future self. I wrote for the moment.

And for the first time in twenty years, I felt like I was listening.

prompt: what's the deal with people who say they 'don't read fiction because it's not real'? I want an essay that takes them seriously for a minute before explaining what they're missing
chosen:
The objection sounds reasonable on its face. It echoes a deep-seated cultural bias that values only what can be verified. If a book claims that a man named Holden Caulfield walked through New York City, and no such man existed, then the statement is false. In a world of information overload, where every headline is a claim to be vetted, the instinct to filter out the unverified is efficient. It is a survival mechanism for the mind.

But this instinct applies the wrong test to the wrong object. The person who dismisses fiction for being "not real" is confusing a map with the territory, or a mirror with the face. They are judging the value of a simulation by the standards of a photograph.

To take the objection seriously for a minute, we must acknowledge what it gets right: non-fiction is a record of what happened. It preserves the specific, the accidental, and the unique. When you read a biography of Abraham Lincoln, you are accessing data that could not have been generated by a novelist. The date of the Gettysburg Address, the specific texture of the rain that day, the actual words spoken—these are facts. Fiction cannot replicate the density of reality. A novelist can describe a battle, but they cannot capture the smell of the specific mud on the specific hill where a specific soldier died. In terms of informational yield per page, non-fiction wins. It is dense with truth.

However, the objection fails because it assumes that the purpose of reading is to acquire information. It treats books as databases rather than instruments for understanding human experience.

Fiction is not an attempt to report the world; it is an attempt to model it. A novel is a theory of how people behave under pressure. When you read *The Great Gatsby*, you are not learning about the stock market of 1922. You are learning about the mechanics of desire, the fragility of the American Dream, and the way class anxiety manifests in social behavior. The characters are not real, but the dynamics are. The emotions are not fabricated; they are amplified and isolated so that you can see them clearly.

This is the core of what the skeptic misses: **specificity creates universality.**

A non-fiction article about a divorce might tell you the legal steps, the financial impacts, and the statistical likelihood of regret. It gives you the skeleton. A novel about a divorce gives you the flesh. It shows you the way a person stares at a coffee cup for ten minutes because they cannot stand the silence. It shows you the specific, irrational anger at a partner for buying the wrong brand of milk. These details are not "real" in the biographical sense, but they are true in the phenomenological sense. They are the texture of the experience.

The human mind does not process truth as a list of facts. It processes truth as narrative. We understand the world through stories. We remember events as plots with rising action and resolution. When we lack a narrative framework for a new experience, we are lost. Fiction provides that framework. It allows us to run simulations of lives we will never live. It is a empathy machine.

Consider the difference between reading a report on the Holocaust and reading *The Diary of a Young Girl* or *Night*. The report gives you the numbers: six million dead. The number is so large it becomes abstract, a shape in the sky rather than a weight in the hand. The fiction (or memoir) brings you to a single room, a single child, a single moment of fear. You do not understand the magnitude of the tragedy by knowing the total; you understand it by feeling the weight of one life. The "unreal" element—the artistic shaping, the selection of detail—is precisely what makes the truth accessible.

Furthermore, fiction allows for the exploration of the interior. Non-fiction is often constrained by what can be observed from the outside. A sociologist can describe a family dynamic, but only a novelist can get inside the head of the father who is failing to connect with his son. The inner monologue is the domain of fiction. It is the only place we can see the thoughts that people do not say, the contradictions they hide, the fears they suppress. To dismiss fiction as "not real" is to dismiss the largest part of human existence: the private, silent, internal life.

There is also the matter of time. Non-fiction is bound to the clock. It happens when it happens. Fiction is bound to the clock of consciousness. A single second of terror can stretch for pages. A decade of boredom can be summarized in a sentence. This manipulation of time is not a lie; it is a translation of how time actually feels to a human being. We do not experience life in chronological order. We experience it in bursts of intensity, flashes of memory, and long stretches of waiting. Fiction mirrors this structure.

The person who refuses to read fiction because it is "not real" is making a category error. They are treating art as science, and science as art. They are asking a painting why it doesn’t contain a real landscape. They are asking a song why it doesn’t contain a real voice.

What they are missing is not information. They are missing depth. They are missing the ability to inhabit other perspectives. They are missing the chance to practice their empathy in a low-stakes environment. They are missing the language we use to describe the things that cannot be measured.

Reality is hard. It is chaotic, painful, and often meaningless. Fiction is a place where we can look at reality’s hardest parts, organize them, and give them shape. It is a place where we can ask, "What if?" and "Why?" without the constraint of "But that didn't happen."

The objection "it’s not real" is a defense against vulnerability. Reading a novel requires you to let the author into your head. It requires you to suspend your judgment and trust the illusion. For some, that is too much work. They prefer the safety of the verified, the known, the factual. But in doing so, they have chosen to live in a world without shadows, without whispers, without the quiet, strange truth of what it is to be a person. They have the map, but they have never walked the road.
rejected:
**The Map and the Territory: Why "Not Real" is the Wrong Objection to Fiction**

There is a specific kind of intellectual pride that attaches itself to the consumption of non-fiction. It is a quiet, often unspoken badge of honor. You see it in the way someone holds a book: if it is a biography, a historical account, or a treatise on economics, they hold it with the gravity of a man handling a load-bearing beam. But if you offer them a novel, they often hesitate, and then, if pressed, they offer the standard defense: *"I just don’t have the time for fiction. It’s not real. I want to know what actually happened."*

At first glance, this position seems reasonable. In an era of information overload, where the stakes of misunderstanding the world can be high, prioritizing verified data feels like a moral imperative. Why waste cognitive resources on a made-up story when the real world is full of underreported tragedies, complex geopolitical shifts, and scientific breakthroughs?

If we take this objection seriously for a minute, it appears to be a stance of radical pragmatism. These readers are not saying fiction is *bad*; they are saying it is *irrelevant*. They are operating under a strict empiricist framework: if it cannot be verified by an external source, it does not exist in the realm of utility. From this perspective, fiction is a luxury, a distraction, a time sink that offers no actionable data. It is the equivalent of playing chess against a wall—technically possible, but ultimately pointless if you want to understand the board.

However, this view rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of what "real" means, and more importantly, it misunderstands the function of narrative. To dismiss fiction because it is "not real" is to confuse the map with the territory, and to mistake the texture of experience for a list of coordinates.

The first thing the "non-fiction only" reader misses is **epistemic depth**. Non-fiction tells you *what* happened. Fiction tells you *how it felt* to be there.

Consider the difference between reading a historical account of the fall of the Berlin Wall and reading a novel set in 1989 East Berlin. The history book can give you the date, the political causes, the casualty count, and the diplomatic fallout. It can give you the facts. But it cannot give you the specific, suffocating anxiety of a father checking the border for his son. It cannot convey the smell of the cigarette smoke in the checkpoint, or the specific, irrational hope that flickers in a citizen’s mind when they hear a rumor.

Fiction is the technology of empathy. It is a simulation of consciousness. When we read a novel, we are not just processing information; we are inhabiting a subjective point of view. We learn not just that people in other cultures or times had different values, but *why* those values felt necessary to them. We learn the logic of their irrationality. Non-fiction can tell you that a character in a tragedy was "angry"; fiction can show you the precise, jagged edge of that anger, and why it was the only sane response to an insane situation. By rejecting fiction, these readers are rejecting the most powerful tool we have for understanding the human condition. They are left with the skeleton of history, but none of the flesh.

The second thing they miss is **the architecture of pattern recognition**. Humans do not think in facts; we think in stories. Our brains are narrative processors. We make sense of the world by organizing it into plots with causes, conflicts, and resolutions. Non-fiction, by its nature, often disrupts this flow. It is fragmented, cited, and dense. Fiction, however, distills complex social dynamics into manageable, resonant patterns.

A great novel is not a lie; it is a hypothesis. It asks, "What if?" It allows us to test our moral intuitions against hypothetical scenarios without real-world consequences. When you read a thriller, you are not just killing time; you are practicing vigilance. When you read a literary novel about a crumbling marriage, you are not just observing a relationship; you are analyzing the mechanics of love, betrayal, and forgiveness in a controlled environment. Fiction allows us to rehearse for life. It is the flight simulator of the soul. Without it, we are navigating the complex, high-stakes environment of actual human interaction without having ever practiced the maneuvers.

Finally, there is the matter of **truth**. The most profound irony of the "fiction is not real" argument is that fiction is often where we find the *truest* truths.

Facts are static. They can be wrong, incomplete, or misleading. But a well-crafted story reveals the emotional and psychological truths that data cannot capture. The "real" world is chaotic, messy, and often illogical. Fiction imposes order on that chaos, not to hide it, but to make it comprehensible. When a novelist writes about grief, they are not providing a medical definition of bereavement; they are articulating the experience of it in a way that resonates with the reader’s own hidden, unspoken grief. This is a deeper kind of reality than a statistic. It is the reality of the interior life, which is the only reality any of us ever directly access.

The people who say they "don’t read fiction because it’s not real" are not wrong to value truth. They are just using a very narrow definition of it. They are treating the world as a database to be queried, rather than a human experience to be lived. They are starving themselves of the very thing that makes them human: the ability to imagine, to empathize, and to understand the world from the inside out.

Fiction is not the opposite of reality. It is the lens through which we make reality legible. To reject it is to choose to see the world in black and white, in bullet points, without color, without depth, and without the capacity to truly feel what it means to be alive in it. The real world is messy, contradictory, and deeply emotional. Fiction is where we learn how to handle all of that.

prompt: An essay arguing that the best writing advice ever given is 'read it out loud' and that almost every other rule is a special case of it.
chosen:
The most reliable editor you will ever have is not a person, a style guide, or a software algorithm. It is your own ear.

When you write, you are engaged in a high-stakes act of translation. You are converting a mental image, a feeling, or a logical structure into a sequence of linear symbols. The brain is remarkably good at this, but it is also remarkably forgiving. It fills in gaps. It skips over stuttering. It assumes the reader knows what you meant because *you* know what you meant. This is the primary failure mode of writing: it is a closed loop.

Reading your work aloud breaks the loop.

The ear is a stricter judge than the eye. The eye scans for meaning; it looks for the expected word and moves on. The ear listens for rhythm, breath, and friction. When you speak a sentence, you must commit to its structure. You cannot "see" your way past a run-on sentence. You physically cannot breathe through a clause that is too long without gasping, and that gasp is a signal that the sentence needs a period, a comma, or a rewrite.

This is why "read it out loud" is not just one piece of advice among many. It is the mechanism that makes all other advice actionable.

Consider the rule: "Avoid passive voice." Most writers know this rule intellectually. They can identify a passive construction in a test question. But in the heat of drafting, the passive voice often feels smoother because it allows the writer to hide behind the action. The passive voice is also frequently clunky. It adds syllables. It obscures the agent. When you read a passive sentence aloud, you will often hear the weight of the extra words. You will feel the distance between the doer and the deed. The ear detects the drag. The fix is rarely to force a passive sentence into active voice for the sake of a rule; it is to shorten the sentence until the agent is front and center, which is usually the active voice. The rule is the destination; the ear is the compass.

Consider the rule: "Vary your sentence length." This is often given as an aesthetic platitude. Writers try to alternate short and long sentences mechanically, resulting in choppy, staccato prose that feels like a march. But if you read your draft aloud, you hear the monotony. A paragraph where every sentence has the same cadence is like a song with no dynamics. It drags. Your ear tells you where the rhythm has stalled. You might find that you don't need a shorter sentence; you need to cut three words from the middle of a long one to restore the beat. The ear detects the rhythm, not just the length.

Consider the rule: "Cut your adverbs." Adverbs are often used to compensate for weak verbs. "He ran quickly" is weaker than "He sprinted." But sometimes an adverb is necessary. The problem is that adverbs often sit at the end of a sentence, where they are easy to ignore on the page. When you speak the sentence, the adverb is the last thing to land. If the verb was strong, the adverb feels like a redundant echo. If the verb was weak, the adverb feels like a band-aid. Either way, the ear catches the awkwardness.

Consider the rule: "Be concise." This is the hardest rule to follow because brevity is not just about word count; it is about information density. A short sentence can be empty. A long sentence can be dense. Reading aloud reveals the density. If you have to stop and think about what a phrase means before you can say it, it is too complex. If you stumble over a phrase, it is too convoluted. If you can say it smoothly, the logic is likely clear.

The ear also detects tone. Writing is a performance. It is you, speaking to an absent other. If you read your draft aloud, you will hear your own voice. You will hear the arrogance, the whining, the false confidence, or the false humility. You will hear the difference between the person you are trying to be in the writing and the person you are in the room. This is a level of feedback that no software can provide. Grammar checkers can tell you that a comma is missing. They cannot tell you that you sound insufferable.

There are exceptions, of course. Poetry, for example, relies on visual layout and the interplay between sound and silence in ways that a single speaker reading aloud might miss. Collaborative writing, where multiple voices are involved, requires a different kind of listening. But for the vast majority of prose—essays, novels, nonfiction, letters, emails—the ear is the final gatekeeper.

The process is simple. Write the draft without caring about the sound. Let the thoughts flow. Then, stop. Read it aloud. Not in your head. Actually move your mouth. Listen. Where do you stumble? Where do you rush? Where do you sigh? Those are the places that need work.

Most writing advice is a set of heuristics derived from what sounds good. "Show, don't tell" is good because telling is often abstract and distant, while showing is concrete and immediate. "Trust your reader" is good because over-explaining breaks the rhythm and insults the listener. "Start in the middle of the action" is good because a slow start is a slow start, and you can hear the drag.

You do not need to memorize a hundred rules. You need to learn to trust your ear. The ear knows when the writing is working. It knows when it is not. It is the most honest critic you have. It does not care about your intentions. It only cares about what comes out of your mouth. And what comes out of your mouth is what the reader hears.
rejected:
**The Ear as the Ultimate Editor: Why "Read It Out Loud" Is the Only Rule That Matters**

In the pantheon of writing advice, there is a mountain of accumulated wisdom. We are told to kill our darlings, to show not tell, to avoid passive voice, to vary sentence length, and to watch out for adverbs. We are handed style guides like bibles and beta readers like priestesses. But beneath the noise of specific techniques lies a singular, ancient, and devastatingly effective command: **Read it out loud.**

If you had to throw every other rule into the fire and keep only one, keep this. It is not merely a proofreading trick for catching typos; it is a fundamental diagnostic tool for rhythm, clarity, and truth. Almost every other piece of writing advice you have ever heard is, at its core, a special case of what your ear detects when you speak your words to the air.

### The Physics of Breath

The human voice is not a digital stream; it is a biological instrument constrained by lungs. When you read a sentence silently, your brain processes it as data. You can skip over clunky phrasing because your mind fills in the gaps. But when you read it aloud, your lungs demand a breath. If a sentence is too long, too convoluted, or structurally dense, you will physically gasp or stumble.

This is why the advice "keep your sentences short" is a special case of reading aloud. It isn’t that short sentences are inherently superior—Hemingway and Faulkner prove otherwise—but that *readable* sentences align with the natural rhythm of breathing. If you find yourself holding your breath to get through a clause, that clause is broken. The ear knows what the eye ignores.

### The Test of Clarity

"Show, don’t tell" is often interpreted as a ban on stating emotions or facts. But its deeper purpose is efficiency and immediacy. When you read a vague, abstract passage aloud, it often sounds dull, flat, or repetitive. The ear is a detector for redundancy.

Consider this: *"He was feeling very sad and depressed about the loss of his job."*
Silently, this is acceptable. Aloud, it drags. The repetition of "sad" and "depressed" hits the ear like a bump in the road. The voice instinctively wants to say: *"The job was gone, and the weight of it crushed him."* The second version has more texture, more weight. The ear rejects the first because it lacks musicality; it rejects the second because it resonates. "Show, don’t tell" is simply the instruction to create prose that has enough sonic and textural variety to keep the listener engaged.

### The Passive Voice Trap

"Why is this passive?" is a common question in editing. But why do we hate passive voice? Not because it’s morally wrong, but because it’s often awkward to say. Passive voice obscures the actor, forcing the listener to search for the subject.

*"The ball was thrown by John."*
Silently, it’s fine. Aloud, it feels like the sentence is hiding something. The voice wants the subject first: *"John threw the ball."* The ear prefers the direct, active connection between agent and action because it mimics the way we experience the world: we do things to things. When a sentence feels like it’s being done *to* the reader rather than *by* a clear subject, it usually sounds clunky. The ear detects the lack of agency before the brain even registers the grammatical term.

### Rhythm and Flow

The most sophisticated writers understand that prose is music. They play with cadence, alliteration, and stress. This is where "read it aloud" becomes not just a check, but a composition tool.

If you read a paragraph and your voice monotonously drones, the paragraph is boring. If your voice naturally rises and falls, creates pauses, and lands with impact, the paragraph works. This is why varying sentence length is crucial. A series of sentences of the same length creates a robotic, metronomic beat. But a short sentence. Followed by a long, winding sentence that meanders through clauses and sub-clauses to build tension, only to snap back with a final, punchy word. That is music. Your ear is the conductor. It tells you when the rhythm is flat and when it’s dynamic.

### The Truth Detector

Finally, reading aloud is a test for authenticity. It is much harder to lie to yourself when you have to hear your own voice. If a sentence feels pretentious, arrogant, or overwrought, it will sound that way out loud. The ear is a social organ; it is tuned to how humans actually speak to each other.

If you write a paragraph that you are proud of, but when you read it aloud, you cringe, you know it’s failed. It’s too much. It’s trying too hard. The ear knows the difference between confidence and posturing. It knows when you’re performing and when you’re communicating.

### Conclusion

Style guides change. Trends shift. What was considered elegant in 1950 is considered stiff in 2020. But the human ear has not changed. The need for clarity, rhythm, and breath is as old as language itself.

So, when you finish a draft, close your eyes. Turn off your inner monologue. And read it out loud. Let your voice stumble. Let your lungs protest. Let your ear tell you what is broken.

Because at the end of the day, writing is not about the page. It is about the voice. And the best writing advice ever given is simply this: **Listen to what your voice is trying to say.**

prompt: Blog essay: why I stopped finishing books I don't like, and why it took me until 41 to give myself permission. Light tone, but I want a real point about what we owe authors (if anything).
chosen:
I am forty-one years old. I have just put down a 400-page novel at page 80. The protagonist is insufferable, the prose is purple, and I have spent three weeks pretending to be interested in a world I find boring.

For decades, finishing a bad book was a badge of honor. It was proof of grit. If you read the last page, you had completed the circuit. You had honored the author’s labor. You had "done" the book.

This was a lie. And I needed to be an adult to believe it.

The permission slip didn’t arrive with a bang. It crept in. I was sitting on a park bench, reading a literary fiction debut that felt like chewing on wet cardboard. I looked at the page count remaining. Two hundred and fifty pages. I looked at my phone. I had a project due in two hours.

I closed the book. I didn’t guiltily text a friend to complain. I didn’t write a review. I just went home, showered, and started my project. The sky didn’t fall. The author didn’t call to demand restitution.

The discomfort I felt in those final minutes wasn’t about the book. It was about the violation of a social contract I had signed without realizing it. The contract says: *If an author spends three years building a world, you owe them your attention for as long as it takes to traverse it.*

We do not owe authors this.

We owe them respect, sure. We owe them the chance to be heard. But we do not owe them our time. Time is the only resource you cannot get back. When you force yourself through a book that isn’t working for you, you are not paying a debt. You are stealing from yourself. You are trading a live, engaged hour for a dead, passive one, and calling it discipline.

Think about why we finish books we hate. Usually, it’s sunk cost. I’ve already read fifty pages; I can’t stop now. That is financial logic applied to art, and it is nonsense. A bad investment should be cut. A bad book should be closed.

There is a second reason, too, and it’s more insidious: we confuse consumption with understanding. We think that if we don’t finish the book, we don’t "know" it. We are afraid of being asked, "Did you read *X*?" and having to say, "No, I stopped." So we finish it to protect our identity as a reader. We finish it to keep up with the book club. We finish it because we are terrified that if we quit, we’ll never start again.

But quitting a bad book is how you keep reading good ones.

When I stopped finishing bad books, I didn’t read less. I read more. I cleared the clutter. I stopped hoarding unfinished novels on my nightstand like shameful secrets. I realized that a book is a relationship, not a task. If the chemistry isn’t there, you don’t force a date. You don’t sit in a bad restaurant for four hours because you paid for the appetizer. You leave.

This doesn’t mean we should be casual with literature. It means we should be honest. If a book isn’t speaking to you, it isn’t your fault. It isn’t the author’s fault. It’s just a mismatch.

The authors I love—those who write books that stay with me for years—they don’t need you to suffer through the middle of their work to prove you’re a good person. They need you to be in the room when the sparks fly. If the sparks aren’t flying, you’re doing them a disservice by forcing your eyes to the page. You’re not honoring their craft. You’re just enduring it.

I am forty-one. I have a full library of books I never finished. I don’t feel like a failure. I feel like I finally have a life.

So, if you’re stuck on page 80 of a book that isn’t working, put it down. Close it. Walk away.

You don’t owe the author your boredom. You owe yourself your attention. And right now, your attention is better spent on something that keeps you up.
rejected:
The dust jacket was beautiful. It was a deep, bruised purple with silver foil that caught the light in a way that suggested the book inside was going to change my life. Or at least make my evenings feel more sophisticated.

For the first forty-one years of my life, I treated that beautiful cover as a contract.

I bought the book. I read the first chapter. I read the second. By chapter three, I was doing that specific type of squinting where you stare at the words on the page and realize they are just shapes, not meaning. The protagonist was insufferable. The plot was a meandering swamp. The author seemed to think that describing the texture of a wall for four pages was a valid narrative device.

But I kept reading. I kept reading until my eyes burned. I kept reading until the book felt like a physical weight on my chest. I kept reading because I had *already started*.

I did this for decades. I finished *The Count of Monte Cristo* (a masterpiece) and I finished that mid-list thriller about a psychic detective who also happens to be a baker (a disaster). I treated them with the same religious devotion. I felt a nagging, guilty twinge in my gut every time I closed a book I hadn’t loved, as if I had abandoned a pet in the rain.

Then, last Tuesday, I put down a 500-page novel on page 40. I closed the cover. I felt a spike of panic. *But I’ve already read 40 pages.* I looked at the book. I looked at my free evening. I realized I was tired. I realized I was bored. And then, for the first time in my adult life, I felt a surge of pure, unadulterated relief.

I didn’t finish it. I haven’t finished it. And I don’t think I ever will.

***

This is the great secret of the reading world that we don’t talk about enough: **We do not owe authors our suffering.**

There is a pervasive cultural myth that finishing a book is a moral obligation. It’s a badge of honor. “I read *War and Peace*,” people say, and there’s a subtext that says, *“Look how much pain I endured for art. I am disciplined. I am cultured.”*

But why?

When I was younger, I thought it was about respect. I thought that by abandoning a book, I was dismissing the author’s labor. I was saying, *“Your words weren’t good enough to keep my attention.”* I thought I was being rude.

But here’s the thing: A book is not a conversation. A book is a monologue.

When you buy a book, you are not entering into a dialogue where you must listen to the speaker until they have said everything they want to say. You are paying for an experience. You are buying an afternoon. You are buying a window into a specific mind, a specific world, a specific way of seeing.

If that window is broken, you walk away.

If the mind is chaotic, you close the door.

If the world feels like a place you don’t want to live for the next six hours, you leave.

We owe authors nothing but our honest attention *while we are there*. We owe them our critical eye. We owe them the chance to speak, but we do not owe them our endurance.

In fact, I’d argue that we owe *ourselves* more than we owe them.

Our time is finite. Our attention is a scarce resource. When we force ourselves to finish a bad book, we are not honoring the author. We are punishing ourselves. We are taking the hours we could have spent reading a book that makes our heart sing, or a book that makes us think, or a book that makes us laugh, and we are pouring them into a black hole of mediocrity.

We are robbing Peter to pay Paul, where Peter is our joy and Paul is our guilt.

***

I’m not saying we should be casual about books. I’m not saying we should treat literature like fast food. I think there is a deep, genuine pleasure in pushing through the difficult parts of a great book. There is a specific kind of satisfaction in wrestling with a dense, complex narrative and emerging on the other side, changed.

But that pleasure comes from the *struggle*, not from the *obligation*.

There’s a difference between “This is hard, but it’s worth it” and “This is hard, and I feel like a failure if I stop.”

I’ve always confused the two.

I think I held onto this idea because it was safer. If I had to finish every book I started, then I didn’t have to make hard choices. I didn’t have to decide which books were truly worth my time. I could just default to “finish it” and avoid the judgment.

But at 41, I’m tired of avoiding judgment. I’m tired of the guilt. I’m tired of looking at my bookshelf and seeing a graveyard of half-read novels that I kept around as monuments to my own stubbornness.

So now, I have a rule. It’s simple.

If I haven’t felt a spark of interest by the third chapter, I stop.

If I’m not enjoying the voice, I stop.

If I’m skimming because I can’t wait for it to be over, I stop.

And when I stop, I don’t feel guilty. I feel light. I feel like I’ve just saved myself five hours of my life.

And then I pick up another book. Maybe it’s a classic. Maybe it’s a genre piece. Maybe it’s a book I’ve been meaning to read for years. But it’s a choice. It’s a choice I make with open eyes, not a contract I signed with a pen I was too polite to refuse.

We don’t owe authors our lives. We owe them our curiosity. And if they don’t earn it, we move on.

And honestly? The world is full of good books. We don’t need to suffer to find them. We just need to let go of the ones that aren’t.

prompt: So I just got back from two weeks in Lisbon and the thing I can't stop thinking about is how every neighborhood I walked through had the same three businesses: a specialty coffee place, a brunch spot with avocado toast, and a shop selling tinned fish in pretty packaging. My friend says that's just what tourism does and I should get over it. But I'm not sure it's that simple, because some of the locals seemed to like it too? Could you write an essay that actually wrestles with this instead of just complaining about gentrification. I want something more honest than the usual take.
chosen:
The tinned fish shop is not a metaphor. It is a business model.

For decades, Lisbon’s economy ran on two engines: tourism and state subsidies. The former brought the money, but it treated the city as a backdrop for a sunset. The latter kept the lights on while the infrastructure crumbled. When the Eurozone crisis hit, the subsidies dried up, and the city was left with a choice: decline or adapt. They chose to adapt by turning the backdrop into the product.

Your observation of the "trifecta"—specialty coffee, avocado toast, tinned fish—is accurate because it reflects a specific kind of urban development that has spread from New York to London to Seoul. It is not gentrification in the traditional sense, which implies the displacement of the old by the new. It is something more insidious: the commodification of the local identity itself.

The tinned fish shop is the key here. *Sardinha* is a national symbol. By packaging it in a matte black box with a minimalist logo, the shop is not selling food; it is selling the *idea* of being in Lisbon. It is a souvenir that functions as a lifestyle marker. The coffee shop is not competing with the local *pastelaria* on taste; it is competing on ambiance, targeting the demographic that pays for the vibe rather than the bean. The brunch spot is a service industry dressed up as a cultural trend.

Your friend is right that tourism drives this, but wrong that it is only a reaction to outsiders. The "locals" who like it are often part of the same economic cohort as the tourists. They are young, educated, and increasingly disconnected from the traditional Lisbon of their grandparents. For them, the avocado toast is not an invasion; it is a signal of cosmopolitan belonging. It is a way to participate in a global urban culture while living in a historic European capital. The friction is not between "locals" and "tourists," but between two different definitions of what Lisbon is.

The older generation, the ones who remember the revolution and the austerity, view these shops as a betrayal. They see the *pastelaria* replaced by a barista machine as a loss of dignity. The younger generation sees the *pastelaria* as quaint, inefficient, and lacking in "brand equity." Both are correct within their own frames of reference.

This creates a city that is bifurcated. In Alfama, the tourist walks past the tinned fish shop and the coffee bar to reach the viewpoint. The view is real, but the context is curated. In Chiado, the same shops appear, but the clientele is mixed. Locals and tourists share the same space, drinking the same oat milk latte, eating the same avocado toast. This is not displacement; it is convergence. The city has become a shared stage where the script is written in the language of global consumerism.

Is this bad? It depends on what you value. If you value authenticity in the sense of unmediated tradition, yes, it is a loss. The tinned fish shop does not honor the sardine; it exploits it. The coffee shop does not respect the *pastelaria*; it obsoletes it. But if you value economic vitality and the ability of a city to sustain itself in a globalized world, the trifecta is a success. It has kept the shops open, the streets clean, and the wages rising.

The discomfort you feel is real, but it is not unique to Lisbon. It is the discomfort of watching a place become a brand. The brand is consistent, safe, and marketable. It is also hollow. The sardine inside the tin is the same sardine that has been sold in Lisbon for centuries. The difference is that now, it is sold to you as an experience. And you bought it. That is the honest truth of the matter. You are not just a visitor; you are a participant in the economy that is reshaping the city. The locals who like it are not fooled; they are just playing a different role in the same game.
rejected:
The Lisbon paradox is less about the food and more about the mirror.

When you walk through Alfama or the Bairro Alto, you are greeted by a triad that has become the global visual language of "authentic modernity": the third-wave coffee shop with the exposed brick and the oat milk options, the brunch spot where the avocado toast is sliced with surgical precision, and the boutique retailing tinned sardines in pastel tins. To the outsider, this feels like a betrayal—a dilution of the soul. Your friend is right that tourism drives this, but they are missing the nuance of *why* the locals didn’t run these businesses away.

The standard narrative of gentrification suggests a simple replacement: the old goes, the new comes, the locals are priced out or displaced, and the neighborhood becomes a museum for the wealthy. But in Lisbon, and increasingly in cities like Melbourne, London, and Brooklyn, the reality is more complex. It is a case of **cultural translation** rather than cultural erasure.

Consider the tinned fish shop. Is it just a souvenir? For the tourist, yes. But for the local, it is a modernization of a grandmother’s pantry. For decades, *sardinha* was a utilitarian food, eaten with bread and wine, often straight from the can on the street. By packaging it beautifully, labeling it with English descriptions, and placing it in a curated shop, the business didn’t kill the tradition; it elevated it into a gift. It made the local habit legible to the outside world without changing the product itself. The locals who buy from these shops aren’t necessarily buying because they think it’s trendy; they are buying because the product is high-quality, the price is reasonable, and the presentation respects the ingredient. They are participating in the same market as the tourist, not being excluded from it.

The same can be said for the coffee and the brunch. It is easy to look at an avocado toast and see only a hollow, Instagrammable cliché. But in the context of a city that has historically had a strong café culture, the rise of specialty coffee is often a local phenomenon first. Many of the best coffee roasters in Lisbon are run by Portuguese baristas who are passionate about the bean. The "brunch spot" often serves a dual purpose: it is a place for the tourist to consume a Western ritual, but it is also a place for the local creative class—designers, tech workers, artists—to gather. The avocado toast is not a substitute for *bifana* or *pastel de nata*; it is an addition to it. It expands the culinary vocabulary of the neighborhood without erasing the old words.

What makes this situation in Lisbon particularly interesting is the economic reality. For many of these businesses, the tourist is the *only* customer who makes the math work. A neighborhood café that serves only locals at high quality prices often cannot sustain itself. The influx of tourism provides the capital that allows a local entrepreneur to open a shop, hire staff, and pay rent. This creates a hybrid economy where the local and the tourist coexist. The local benefits from the infrastructure and the economic vitality; the tourist benefits from the access to a curated, "authentic" experience. It is a transaction, yes, but not necessarily an exploitative one.

However, the discomfort you feel is not irrational. It stems from the **homogenization of aesthetic**. The danger is not that the local food has disappeared, but that the *presentation* of the city has become standardized. When every neighborhood looks the same—exposed brick, black metal frames, same fonts on the menu—the unique character of the place risks being flattened. The risk is that the local stops making things *for* the local and starts making things *for* the camera. When the avocado toast is made primarily to be photographed, it ceases to be food and becomes a prop. That is where the authenticity dies.

But is that happening in Lisbon? Not entirely. The reason the locals seem to like it is that they are still in control of the narrative. They are the ones choosing which tins to sell, which beans to roast, and how to slice the avocado. The global trends are being adopted, but they are being filtered through local taste and local economic needs. The local is not a passive victim of globalization; they are an active participant, using the tools of the global market to sustain their community.

The honest take is not that this is good or bad, but that it is **inevitable and adaptive**. Cities are living organisms, and they metabolize new inputs. Lisbon has taken the global trend of specialty coffee and curated retail and metabolized it, turning it into a source of income and cultural pride. The fact that you saw the same three businesses in every neighborhood is not proof of a soulless clone; it is proof of a successful local business model that resonates with both the insider and the outsider.

Your friend says you should get over it. They are partly right. The complaint about "authenticity" is often a complaint about change itself, about the loss of a static, romanticized past that never existed. The past was not a museum; it was a struggle. The present is not a betrayal; it is a negotiation.

So, what should you do with this knowledge? Stop expecting the city to be a postcard. Accept that Lisbon is a global city that speaks multiple languages. The tinned fish is still sardine. The coffee is still roasted. The toast is still bread and avocado. The neighborhood has not been replaced; it has been updated. And if the locals are there, smiling and paying for the same things you are, then perhaps the compromise is working. The soul of the city isn’t in the objects it sells, but in the people who choose to keep buying them.

prompt: Contrarian take I want developed into a blog post: suburbs get unfairly mocked by people who grew up in them and moved away. Defend the cul-de-sac. Not ironically.
chosen:
The sneer toward the cul-de-sac is a specific brand of post-migration amnesia.
